think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: The patient presents with a chronic, 2-year evolution of widespread, confluent nodulocutaneous lesions affecting the face, trunk, and extremities, accompanied by superficial mucosal lesions of the nose and lip. This extensive presentation creates a major clinical diagnostic challenge in differentiating disseminated cutaneous leishmaniasis (a hyperergic, metastatic form caused by Viannia subgenus parasites) from diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis (an anergic form characterized by lepromatoid plaques, high parasite loads, absence of mucosal involvement, and negative leishmanin skin tests).
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission triage phase ends after establishing the patient's geographic origin, the 2-year symptom chronology spanning initial forearm inoculation to trunk, extremity, and facial spread, the physical examination demonstrating confluent lesions with mucosal extension, and prior incomplete outpatient therapy. It stops immediately before leishmanin skin testing, serology, lesion smear microscopy, and molecular PCR identification.
3. Differential Distinctions: Diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis (DCL) occurs in the setting of defective cellular immunity, exhibiting negative Montenegro skin tests, abundant amastigotes in tissue, absence of mucosal involvement, and high resistance to antimonial therapy. In contrast, disseminated cutaneous leishmaniasis displays preserved cellular immunity (strong Montenegro reaction), scanty amastigotes, potential mucosal spread, and good clinical response to antimonials. Localized cutaneous leishmaniasis is excluded by the sheer multi-segmental cutaneous dissemination and mucosal invasion.
case_prompt:
A 43-year-old man from a small rural community in Chimborazo province, Ecuador—a subtropical mountainous area situated at the base of the Andean slopes at an altitude of 500 meters above sea level—presented for evaluation of chronic, widespread cutaneous lesions with mucosal involvement. The patient had a history of chronic alcohol consumption.

The illness began approximately two years prior with an insect bite-like papular lesion on the forearm. Subsequently, additional lesions appeared on his right ear and nose. Over the next two years, the disease progressed significantly, with eruptive lesions spreading across extensive areas of his lower extremities, followed by multiple and confluent lesions developing over his abdomen, thorax, flanks, and thighs. He had received a series of empiric injections at a rural health center without lasting resolution, and was referred to a specialized institute for comprehensive diagnostic evaluation.

On physical examination, the patient had widespread cutaneous disease featuring multiple, confluent papulonodular lesions distributed across the thorax, abdomen, flanks, and thighs, along with prominent facial lesions on the right ear and nose. In addition, there was distinct superficial involvement of the mucosae of the nose and upper lip. Systemic examination and initial admission workup were initiated.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to the extensive, confluent papulonodular lesions covering the trunk and extremities. Ruled out by the presence of superficial mucosal involvement of the nose and lip (which does not occur in diffuse CL), intact delayed-type hypersensitivity on skin testing (17-mm induration), responsiveness to antimonials, and molecular identification of Leishmania (Viannia) guyanensis rather than an anergic Leishmania mexicana complex species.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Thus, the case was clinically very similar to diffuse-CL but showed the following marked differences: (1) the organisms isolated were identified as the subgenus Viannia, L. (V.) guyanensis, which is also known as one of the causative agents of disseminated-CL in different endemic countries of the New World; (2) the patient was sensitive against antimonials; and (3) the superficial involvement of mucosae was recognized as seen in Fig. 2c, such a mucosal sign is never seen in diffuse-CL cases.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered early during the single insect-bite-like papular stage on the forearm; excluded by the subsequent two-year multi-anatomic dissemination across the lower extremities, thorax, abdomen, ears, nose, and mucosal surfaces.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The lesion began with an insect bite-like papular lesion on the forearm. Then, the lesions appeared on the right ear and the nose. About 2 years later, lesions appeared on a wide range of the lower extremities, followed by multiple and confluent lesions on the abdomen, thorax, body side, and thigh (photographs not shown). A superficial involvement of mucosae of the nose and upper lip was observed as seen in Fig. 4a.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Detection of scanty intracellular amastigotes on smear examination of active lesions, accompanied by a robust 17-mm positive Montenegro delayed-type hypersensitivity skin reaction and definitive PCR identification of Leishmania (Viannia) guyanensis from biopsy and FTA card specimens, confirming disseminated cutaneous leishmaniasis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Montenegro skin test showed positive with a 17-mm induration, and rK39 kit test revealed a strongly positive band, suggesting a higher level of functions of the humoral immune system(s)... The smear specimen revealed positive for the Leishmania amastigote with a scanty number... The parasites from the biopsy and FTA  card materials were identified as L. (V.) guyanensis by PCR analysis (Fig. 3).

editor_comments: Admission narrative strictly adheres to the admission breakpoint with zero mention of pathogen names, antimonial therapy, or confirmatory skin tests/PCR. The differential distinctions focus on resolving the classic diagnostic dilemma between diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis and disseminated cutaneous leishmaniasis, supported by verbatim quotes.
